newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lankan troops target rebels' jungle lairs.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lankan troops target rebels' jungle lairs.

text.p: Sri Lankan forces, who have seized the last major town controlled by the Tamil Tigers, will launch a push into the rebels' jungle lairs before the guerrillas can regain strength, a top defence official said on Friday.

Deputy Defence Minister Anuruddha Ratwatte said the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) would try to build power for a repeat of July's capture of a key army camp, in which well over 1,000 soldiers were killed or taken hostage.
"We don't intend to permit them to do so," he told a news conference.

Ratwatte, the most powerful military official after President Chandrika Kumaratunga who also holds the defence portfolio, said the rebel strength had been reduced to around 3,000 to 4,000 fighters from an estimated 10,000 in April last year.

He described the capture on Sunday of the rebel's stronghold of Kilinochchi, the last major town under rebel control, as a big victory that could pave the way for a peace settlement in the 13-year ethnic war.
The LTTE, which is fighting the largely Sinhalese troops for a separate homeland for minority Tamils, had fallen back to their jungle bases in the northern mainland Wanni region.
"They go to the jungle and we follow them there," he said.
Ratwatte did not rule out peace talks with the LTTE but said any negotiations would require rebels laying down their arms and setting up a timeframe for a settlement.
He accused the LTTE of using dialogue in the past to gain time to "reorganise, train and arm themselves to come back on war".
Army chief Lieutenant General Rohan Daluwatte told the same news conference that troops were busy re-establishing a base at Kilinochchi and preparing for the return of civilians there.
Kilinochchi is the northern entry point of a large swathe of rebel jungle territory in the Wanni which divides the northern Jaffna peninsula from the rest of the island.
"Having lost Jaffna, the most important place as far as the terrorists were concerned, was Kilinochchi," Daluwatte said.
He said the rebels had put up stiff resistance in which 575 rebels were killed and more than 1,000 wounded. The army lost about 250 soldiers in the eight-day offensive, he said.
The LTTE has so far said only 90 of its fighters died. With reporters banned from the war zone, no independent verification is possible.
The Tigers set up a base in Kilinochchi in April after the army captured Jaffna, which had been ruled by rebels for almost a decade with their own administration, courts and police.
Ratwatte said the military would try to reopen a highway though 70 km (45 miles) of rebel territory to secure a land supply route to Jaffna, which is now supplied by air and sea.
"That is a requirement...We want to open up all the highway and make life normal," he said.

Diplomats and defence analysts have doubted whether the army can reopen the highway to Jaffna. "The troops are just spread too thin for them to make such a huge thrust and sustain it," one Asian diplomat said.
Diplomats said about 30 percent of the 100,000-strong army was already tied up in Jaffna to maintain security there.
